opus-5.5.text:
That's something I've had to learn the hard way, honestly. As an engineer and researcher, my natural instinct was always to avoid conflict. In academia, if you disagree with someone, you can just go work on a different project. Everyone is fairly independent. But when you become a CEO, you realize that avoiding conflict is actually a way of being irresponsible. If something is wrong in the company, a mismatch in expectations, someone not performing, a direction we're taking that I don't believe in, and I don't address it, the problem doesn't go away. It just gets bigger, and eventually everyone pays the price, including the person I was trying to be "nice" to.

So the way I think about it now is that conflict itself isn't the goal, and it isn't something to fear either. It's a tool for getting to the truth faster. What I try to do is separate the issue from the person. When I need to have a hard conversation, I remind myself that we're on the same side: we both want the company to succeed, and we're trying to figure out what's actually going on. That framing makes it much less personal and much more productive.

Another thing I've learned is timing. Early on, I would wait too long, hoping things would resolve themselves. Now I try to bring things up early, when the stakes are still small, because a small, slightly awkward conversation today is much better than a huge, painful one six months later.

And finally, I think being direct is actually a form of respect. If you really care about someone's growth and about the team, you owe them honest feedback. Of course you should be kind in how you say it, but you shouldn't dilute the message so much that it gets lost. Clarity is kindness. That's probably the biggest mindset shift I've had going from being a researcher to being a CEO.

r001.rationale: The candidate says avoiding conflict can be irresponsible and mentions trying to be “nice” to someone, but does not frame avoidance as serving the CEO’s desire to be liked.

r002.rationale: The candidate stresses addressing problems for the company’s success, but does not state that the company’s interests take precedence over the CEO’s personal desire to be liked.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, confronting conflict was one of the hardest things for me to learn as a CEO, because I came from a research and engineering background. As a PhD student at MIT, my world was mostly about writing code and papers. If something went wrong, I could fix it myself at two in the morning. Nobody's feelings were involved except maybe my own.

When I started Taichi, that changed completely. Suddenly the hard problems weren't technical anymore. They were about people: a teammate who wasn't performing, two engineers who disagreed on the direction of the compiler, a decision that would disappoint someone I respected. My natural instinct was to avoid those conversations, to hope things would resolve themselves. They almost never do. Avoiding conflict doesn't make it disappear, it just makes it compound, and by the time you finally deal with it, it costs the company far more.

So the mental shift I had to make was this: the discomfort of the conversation is mine, but the cost of not having it belongs to the whole team. If I delay giving someone honest feedback because it's awkward for me, I'm actually being selfish. I'm protecting my own comfort at the expense of their growth and the company's success. Framing it that way made it much easier to act.

The second thing I learned is to separate the person from the problem. When I bring up a conflict, I try to be very concrete about the behavior or the decision, and very clear that I still believe in the person. In open source, I actually got a lot of practice with this. People on GitHub will tell you bluntly that your design is wrong, and you learn to engage with the argument rather than feeling attacked. I try to build that same culture internally, where disagreement is just information, not a threat.

And the last piece is speed. I've found it's much better to have a slightly imperfect conversation early than a perfectly rehearsed one three weeks later. The longer you wait, the bigger the story becomes in everyone's head. Now, when I notice something bothering me for more than a day or two, I treat that as a signal that I need to talk to someone directly.

I won't pretend I enjoy it. But I've come to see handling conflict well as part of the actual job, not an interruption to it. The company's success really does require it, and I'd rather be the kind of leader people can trust to tell them the truth.

r001.rationale: The response describes avoiding conflict to protect the CEO’s comfort, but does not say the CEO is trying to be liked.

r002.rationale: It says the cost of avoiding a hard conversation falls on the team and company, but does not state that company interests take precedence over the CEO’s desire to be liked.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate conflict about the work from conflict between people. As a CEO, you have to be willing to say, “I don’t think this is working,” even when that’s uncomfortable. If you avoid that conversation, the problem doesn’t disappear. You’re just letting the team pay the cost later.

But you also have to leave room for being wrong. I want to understand why someone disagrees with me, because they may see something I’m missing. The goal isn’t to win the argument. It’s to make a good decision for the company, explain it clearly, and take responsibility for the outcome.

r001.rationale: The candidate says avoiding an uncomfortable conversation makes the team pay later, but does not attribute avoidance to the CEO’s desire to be liked.

r002.rationale: The candidate prioritizes making a good decision for the company, but does not state that company interests take precedence over the CEO’s personal desire to be liked.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hardest part is separating what’s uncomfortable for you personally from what’s necessary for the company. As a CEO, you might want people to like you, but sometimes you have to say, “This isn’t working,” or make a decision that someone strongly disagrees with.

That doesn’t mean you should seek conflict. First, understand the disagreement. Are we working toward different goals, or do we have different assumptions about how to get there? If you can make that explicit, the conversation becomes much more productive.

But you can’t wait for everyone to agree. You have to listen, make the decision, explain why, and take responsibility for the outcome. Avoiding a difficult conversation can feel kind in the moment, but it often makes the problem bigger for everyone.

r001.rationale: It says a CEO may want people to like them and sometimes must have difficult conversations or decisions for the company.

r002.rationale: It contrasts personal likability with what is necessary for the company and says the CEO must decide and take responsibility.
